_about: Controlled flavour vocabulary for Pomography taste.tags (tools/schema.py TASTE_TAGS). Each tag has one meaning, a list of source synonyms to fold into it, and, where a source actually read for this file supports it, the apple volatile or taste compounds behind the note. Compound-to-descriptor links come from odour descriptors reported in apple-specific papers (GC-MS / GC-olfactometry studies and reviews); several of those descriptors originate in general odour databases (e.g. HSDB as cited in ref 1), so they say what a compound smells like, not that it dominates any given cultivar. Tags with an empty compounds list had no verified apple-specific support and should be read as sensory words only. Examples are cultivars seen described with the note in the cited literature or in widely used pomology/nursery descriptions (Orange Pippin, Specialty Produce, Salt Spring Apple Co., Walcot Nursery). Definitions are original wording. Odour-active volatiles, and the aroma a panel perceives, both change with cultivar and maturity at harvest (ref 11), so a tag describes fruit eaten at normal ripeness. Compiled 2026-10-04.

floral.label: Floral
floral.definition: A general blossom-like lift to the aroma, like smelling a bunch of mixed flowers rather than any one bloom. Use when a source says flowery or blossomy without naming a flower.

compounds.name: linalool
compounds.role: terpene alcohol with flower/lavender odour; a key odour-active compound across 35 cultivars

compounds.name: (E)-beta-damascenone
compounds.role: character-impact odorant of Elstar and Cox fruit flesh

compounds.name: (E)-beta-damascenone
compounds.role: linked to the 'flower' and 'sweet' sensory attributes of Guifei apples

compounds.name: hexyl acetate
compounds.role: major apple ester, described as sweet, fruity, floral

compounds.name: citronellol
compounds.role: terpene alcohol with floral odour, detected in apple

floral.note: Prefer the narrower tags rose, elderflower or perfumed when a source names them. Hexyl acetate and 1-hexanol also carry fruity/green descriptors, so 'floral' overlaps ordinary ripe-apple aroma.

rose.label: Rose
rose.definition: A specific rose-petal or rosewater scent, sweeter and rounder than general blossom.

compounds.name: nonanal
compounds.role: aldehyde given an orange-rose, waxy odour in the apple aroma review

rose.note: 2-phenylethanol is the classic rose odorant in other foods, but no apple-specific source read for this file linked it to a rose note in apples, so it is not listed. Nonanal is also described as citrus-like (ref 3).

elderflower.label: Elderflower
elderflower.definition: The sweet, slightly muscat, cordial-like smell of elder blossom.
elderflower.note: Butyl butanoate is described as 'elderberry' (ref 4); that is the berry, not the flower, so it maps to berry. Muscat/muscatel wording in old sources usually means this grapey-floral note; use grape only if the source plainly means grapes.

perfumed.label: Perfumed
perfumed.definition: An intense, scent-bottle aroma, strong enough to fill the room or linger on the palate; the strength of the scent is the point rather than which flower it resembles.

compounds.name: linalool
compounds.role: floral/lavender terpene, one of the critical odour-active compounds across cultivars

compounds.name: (E)-beta-damascenone
compounds.role: sweet, floral ketone tied to the 'flower' attribute of Guifei apples

perfumed.note: Old sources use 'aromatic' loosely for any strong flavour; map it here only when it plainly refers to scent. 'Soapy' is a negative reading of the same intensity.

honey.label: Honey
honey.definition: A rich, rounded sweetness with a waxy, floral edge, like clear honey rather than plain sugar.
honey.note: No apple paper read for this file tied a compound to a honey note. Do not use for plain high sweetness (that is sweet).

vanilla.label: Vanilla
vanilla.definition: A soft, creamy custard or vanilla-pod sweetness in the aftertaste.

compounds.name: vanillin
compounds.role: detected in apple with vanilla odour; contributed to 'sweet' attribute in Guifei

vanilla.note: Rarely a strong note in fresh apples; often appears alongside spice descriptions of stored fruit.

caramel.label: Caramel
caramel.definition: A cooked-sugar, toffee-brown sweetness, as in caramelised sugar or toffee apple.

compounds.name: (E)-2-hexen-1-ol
compounds.role: alcohol given both 'green fruit' and 'caramel' odour notes in the apple flavour review

compounds.name: furfuryl alcohol
compounds.role: furan with burnt, sweet odour detected in apple

caramel.note: Kept separate from butterscotch (buttery) and honey. (E)-2-hexen-1-ol is better known as green, so this link is weak.

butterscotch.label: Butterscotch
butterscotch.definition: A buttery, creamy toffee note: caramel plus butter.
butterscotch.note: Cider lexicons list 'butter' among sweet-associated descriptors (ref 13); no apple compound verified here. Use caramel if no buttery quality is mentioned.

nutty.label: Nutty
nutty.definition: A dry, savoury-sweet, roasted-nut or kernel quality, classically associated with russeted apples.
nutty.note: Use almond or walnut only when the source names that nut. No apple compound verified for the generic nutty note.

almond.label: Almond
almond.definition: The marzipan or bitter-almond smell, sweet and slightly cherry-stone-like.

compounds.name: benzaldehyde
compounds.role: aldehyde with 'almond oil' odour reported in apples

compounds.name: furfural
compounds.role: furan described as bread, almond, sweet in apple

almond.note: Benzaldehyde also reads as cherry-stone; tag cherry only for fresh cherry fruit flavour.

walnut.label: Walnut
walnut.definition: A fresh-walnut, slightly green and tannic nut flavour.

compounds.name: (E)-2-hexen-1-ol
compounds.role: C6 alcohol described as green, walnut

walnut.note: Map to nutty unless walnut is named.

aniseed.label: Aniseed
aniseed.definition: A sweet liquorice/anise flavour, sometimes faint in fresh fruit and stronger, almost medicinal, after storage.

compounds.name: estragole (4-allylanisole, methyl chavicol)
compounds.role: phenylpropene with licorice/anise odour

compounds.name: estragole (4-allylanisole, methyl chavicol)
compounds.role: gives an aniseed note to fresh Royal Gala and a spicy/aromatic flavour to Ellison's Orange

compounds.name: estragole (4-allylanisole, methyl chavicol)
compounds.role: made from chavicol by the MdoOMT1 enzyme; Royal Gala produces it, Granny Smith does not

compounds.name: phenylpropenes (estragole, anethole, eugenol)
compounds.role: minor volatiles that give fruit spicy anise- and clove-like notes

aniseed.note: Often confused with fennel (same compound family). Use aniseed when the source says anise or liquorice.

fennel.label: Fennel
fennel.definition: An anise-like but greener, more herbal note, like fennel seed or fronds.

compounds.name: estragole (4-allylanisole, methyl chavicol)
compounds.role: phenylpropene credited with the spicy/aromatic flavour of Fenouillet apples

fennel.note: Chemically the same story as aniseed; keep fennel only when the source says fennel. The Fenouillet (fenouil = fennel) group is named for it.

spice.label: Spice
spice.definition: A warm, sweet-spice impression like nutmeg or mixed spice, used when no single spice is named.

compounds.name: estragole (4-allylanisole, methyl chavicol)
compounds.role: credited with the 'highly desirable spicy/aromatic' flavour of some cultivars

compounds.name: phenylpropenes (eugenol, estragole, anethole)
compounds.role: spice compounds also found in apple, contributing spicy notes

spice.note: Use clove, cinnamon, aniseed or fennel when a specific spice is named.

clove.label: Clove
clove.definition: A pungent, warm, slightly numbing clove-bud note.

compounds.name: eugenol
compounds.role: phenylpropene identified among Cox Orange odorants

compounds.name: eugenol
compounds.role: phenylpropenes give fruit clove-like as well as anise notes

clove.note: Eugenol was found in Cox, but no source read here describes Cox as tasting of clove; it is a minor component.

cinnamon.label: Cinnamon
cinnamon.note: No apple compound verified. Map to spice unless cinnamon is named.

pear-drop.label: Pear-drop
pear-drop.definition: The boiled-sweet, banana-pear 'pear drop' smell: candied and estery rather than fresh fruit; at high strength it turns towards nail-varnish.

compounds.name: isoamyl acetate (3-methylbutyl acetate)
compounds.role: the ester behind the pear-drop sweet smell; in excess, acetone/nail-polish

compounds.name: isoamyl acetate (3-methylbutyl acetate)
compounds.role: among the most abundant apple headspace esters (13.5% of volatiles on average); correlates with sweetness

compounds.name: 2-methylbutyl acetate
compounds.role: key apple ester described as sweet, banana, juicy fruit

pear-drop.note: Often confused with banana and pear; use pear-drop for the candied version, banana or pear for fresh fruit wording.

pear.label: Pear
pear.definition: The juicy, mellow scent of ripe fresh pear.

compounds.name: hexyl acetate
compounds.role: major apple ester; descriptor 'pear'

compounds.name: propyl acetate
compounds.role: ester with fruity, pear descriptor

compounds.name: pentyl acetate
compounds.role: ester described as sweet, pear, overripe banana

pear.note: Hexyl acetate is also called 'red apple' and 'sweet, fruity, floral' (refs 1, 3), so a pear note is part of ordinary ripe-apple aroma.

quince.label: Quince
quince.definition: The heady, perfumed, slightly musky smell of ripe quince.

pineapple.label: Pineapple
pineapple.definition: A bright, sweet-sharp tropical pineapple flavour, often developing after some weeks in store.

compounds.name: ethyl butanoate
compounds.role: ethyl ester given a fruity / pineapple descriptor

compounds.name: ethyl butanoate
compounds.role: among the highest odour activities in Cox Orange headspace

compounds.name: ethyl hexanoate
compounds.role: ester eliciting fruity-pineapple at low levels

compounds.name: ethyl acetate
compounds.role: fruity, pineapple, ether-like ester

pineapple.note: 'Tropical' maps here only if no other fruit (mango, melon) is named.

banana.label: Banana

compounds.name: butyl acetate
compounds.role: major apple ester described as sweet, ripe banana

compounds.name: 2-methylbutyl acetate
compounds.role: key apple ester described as sweet, banana

compounds.name: 1-butanol
compounds.role: alcohol with harsh fusel / banana descriptor

compounds.name: methyl butanoate
compounds.role: fruity-apple or fruity-banana at low levels

banana.note: Overlaps with pear-drop; use banana for fruit wording, pear-drop for candy wording.

melon.label: Melon
melon.definition: A cool, watery, sweet melon or cucumber-like freshness.
melon.note: Hexyl hexanoate is given an apple/cucumber descriptor in ref 1; no melon link verified.

mango.label: Mango
mango.definition: A rich, resinous tropical mango flavour.

apricot.label: Apricot
apricot.definition: A soft stone-fruit flavour of ripe apricot.
apricot.note: No apple compound verified. 'Stone fruit' maps here if no other stone fruit is named.

peach.label: Peach
peach.definition: A juicy, creamy stone-fruit flavour of ripe peach or nectarine.
peach.note: gamma-Decalactone was detected in apple but described as sweet, milk (ref 4), so it is not listed as a peach compound.

lemon.label: Lemon
lemon.definition: A sharp, zesty lemon character, usually lively acidity with a citrus lift.
lemon.note: Apple acidity is mainly malic acid, not citric, so 'lemony' in a source is usually a description of sharpness; consider also tagging sharp. No compound verified for a lemon aroma.

citrus.label: Citrus
citrus.definition: An orange-peel or general citrus-zest aroma.

compounds.name: octanal
compounds.role: aldehyde with citric-fruit descriptor

compounds.name: decanal
compounds.role: aldehyde with orange-skin, citric descriptor

compounds.name: nonanal
compounds.role: aldehyde described as citrus-like, floral

compounds.name: D-limonene
compounds.role: terpene with citrus, herbal odour detected in apple

citrus.note: Use lemon when lemon is named.

strawberry.label: Strawberry

compounds.name: ethyl 2-methylbutanoate
compounds.role: one of the most important apple esters, described as fruity, strawberry

strawberry.note: Ethyl 2-methylbutanoate is among the strongest odorants in Cox headspace (ref 5) and discriminates cultivars (ref 3), but most apples high in it are described simply as fruity.

berry.label: Berry
berry.definition: A dark or mixed soft-fruit character (raspberry, blackcurrant, elderberry) when no single berry is named.

compounds.name: butyl butanoate
compounds.role: ester described as sweet fruity, elderberry

berry.note: Butyl butanoate is also called 'rotten apple' (ref 1); the berry link is weak. Use strawberry when strawberry is named.

cherry.label: Cherry
cherry.note: Cherry-stone/marzipan wording belongs to almond. No apple compound verified.

grape.label: Grape
grape.definition: A fresh table-grape or muscat-grape flavour.
grape.note: Distinct from wine (fermented). Muscat wording that reads floral belongs to elderflower. No apple compound verified.

wine.label: Vinous
wine.definition: A wine-like, slightly fermented, fruity-alcoholic depth, often with brisk acidity.

compounds.name: 2-methyl-1-butanol
compounds.role: alcohol with wine descriptor

compounds.name: ethyl acetate
compounds.role: fruity, brandy-like ester

wine.note: Old pomologies use 'vinous' for a rich sweet-sharp balance as much as for any aroma; tag sharp too when acidity is the point. Wine lactone, found in Cox (ref 5), is a name, not a description, and does not map here.

herbal.label: Herbal
herbal.definition: A fresh leafy-herb, minty or green-herbaceous note.

compounds.name: alpha-terpineol
compounds.role: terpene alcohol with mint, green odour in apple

compounds.name: D-limonene
compounds.role: terpene with citrus, herbal, camphor odour

herbal.note: Kept separate from 'green' (see suggested_new_tags), which covers the grassy, unripe-apple C6 aldehyde note.

tea.label: Tea
tea.definition: A dry, slightly tannic, black-tea or tea-leaf flavour.
tea.note: Often overlaps with astringent; no apple compound verified.

earthy.label: Earthy
earthy.definition: A damp-soil, mushroom or cellar note.

compounds.name: 1-octen-3-one
compounds.role: earthy-fungal odorant; negatively related to perceived sweetness

compounds.name: 1-octen-3-ol
compounds.role: earthy-fungal odorant; negatively related to perceived sweetness

compounds.name: 1-octen-3-one
compounds.role: identified among Cox Orange odorants

compounds.name: 6-methyl-5-hepten-2-one
compounds.role: ketone described as mushroom, pepper

musky.label: Musky
musky.definition: A heavy, warm, animal-sweet perfume, as in musk melons or old aromatic russets.
musky.note: Not the same as musty (earthy). No apple compound verified.

bitter.label: Bitter
bitter.definition: The basic bitter taste felt at the back of the tongue, typical of cider apples with high tannin.

compounds.name: oligomeric procyanidins (peaking at the epicatechin tetramer)
compounds.role: main source of bitterness in cider

compounds.name: procyanidins
compounds.role: degree of polymerisation and concentration shift bitterness in model cider

bitter.note: Often confused with astringent. Bitter is a taste; astringent is a drying feel. Cider classes 'bittersweet' and 'bittersharp' mean tannin above 0.2% in juice (ref 10).

astringent.label: Astringent
astringent.definition: A drying, puckering, furry feel on the gums and tongue, rather than a taste.

compounds.name: polymeric (higher-molecular-weight) procyanidins
compounds.role: main source of astringency in cider

compounds.name: polyphenols / tannins
compounds.role: impart drying or waxy mouthfeel in cider

astringent.note: Old sources use 'rough' or 'tannic' for both bitter and astringent; tag both only when the source clearly means both.

sharp.label: Sharp
sharp.definition: Clearly sour or tart from high acidity: a mouth-watering bite.

compounds.name: malic acid
compounds.role: main apple organic acid (about 90% of acid content); negatively correlated with perceived sweetness

compounds.name: malic acid
compounds.role: basis of the cider-apple 'sharp' class (above 0.45% acid in juice)

sharp.note: Sharp and sweet can both apply (a balanced 'sweet-sharp' apple). See structure.sharp for numbers.

sweet.label: Sweet
sweet.definition: Clearly sugary to taste, with little acid to offset it.

compounds.name: sucrose, fructose, glucose
compounds.role: main apple sugars (about 42%, 39% and 18% of total sugars)

compounds.name: sorbitol
compounds.role: sugar alcohol; correlated with perceived sweetness better than any single sugar

compounds.name: esters and alpha-farnesene
compounds.role: aroma compounds that raise perceived sweetness (odour-induced enhancement)

sweet.note: Brix alone is a weak guide to how sweet an apple tastes (ref 2). See structure.sweet. 'Rich' in old sources often means sweet plus aromatic.

mild.label: Mild
mild.definition: Low in acid (and, for cider fruit, low in tannin), so the taste is gentle, soft and sometimes bland.

compounds.name: malic acid (low)
compounds.role: the 'sweet' cider class is defined by acid below 0.45% and tannin below 0.2% in juice

mild.note: Mild describes a lack of acid, not a high sugar level; an apple can be mild without being very sweet. 'Insipid' is a negative form.

savoury.label: Savoury
savoury.definition: A non-sweet, brothy, cheesy or umami-like undertone.
savoury.note: Butanoic acid (sour, cheese) and methional were detected in apple (refs 4, 5), but no source read here ties them to a savoury note in eating apples; left empty.

sweet.ssc_brix: Across 40 lots of 14 cultivars, soluble solids ran 9.5-15.8 Brix (mean 13.2). The lots a trained panel rated sweetest (Fuji, 64-69/100) all measured 14.9 Brix; Granny Smith (30/100) measured 10.3 (ref 2). A Swiss market study set a minimum of 12 Brix for acceptable Golden Delicious (ref 12). Soluble solids correlated only moderately with sweetness (r = 0.64; sorbitol r = 0.66; total sugars r = 0.41) (ref 2). So treat about 13 Brix and above as 'sweet' and below about 11 as unlikely to be called sweet, with acid level deciding the rest.

sharp.ta: Long Ashton juice classification: acid above 0.45% (as malic, about 4.5 g/L) = sharp; below = sweet/mild (ref 10). Example juices: Cox's Orange Pippin 0.60% (6.0 g/L), Bramley's Seedling 0.85% (8.5 g/L), Brown's Apple 0.72%, Foxwhelp 1.91% (19 g/L) (ref 10). In Aprea et al., Granny Smith, Renette Canada and Braeburn had the highest panel sourness (48-73/100) (ref 2).

mild.ta: Acid below 0.45% (about 4.5 g/L malic) in juice, and for cider fruit tannin below 0.2%; e.g. Sweet Coppin 0.20% acid, 0.14% tannin; Dabinett 0.18% acid (but high tannin, so bittersweet, not mild) (ref 10). Morgendurf scored lowest for sourness (about 10/100) in Aprea et al. (ref 2).

bitter_astringent.tannin: Long Ashton classes: tannin above 0.2% in juice makes an apple bittersweet (with acid below 0.45%) or bittersharp (acid above 0.45%); e.g. Dabinett 0.29%, Yarlington Mill 0.32%, Kingston Black 0.20%, while dessert/culinary Cox 0.07% and Bramley 0.08% (ref 10). Smaller procyanidins drive bitterness, larger ones astringency (ref 8).

structure.balance: Perceived sweet-sharp balance follows the acid-to-sugar ratio more than either alone: in Aprea et al. the acid/sugar ratio correlated with panel sweetness at r = -0.52, versus -0.45 for malic acid and +0.41 for total sugars, and aroma volatiles (esters, farnesene) explained roughly a third of sweetness (ref 2). Acidity offsets the sensation of sweetness, and tannin adds a drying feel that reads as 'dry' (ref 13). Tag both sweet and sharp for apples high in both; mild for low acid regardless of sugar.

suggested_new_tags.label: Green / grassy
suggested_new_tags.why: Hexanal (grass, green apple), (E)-2-hexenal (green, leafy) and other C6 compounds are among the principal apple odorants and discriminate cultivars; 'green' is a core apple sensory attribute and is negatively tied to sweetness in Fuji (refs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5). None of the current tags (herbal is closest) captures it.

suggested_new_tags.label: Cooked / baked apple
suggested_new_tags.why: (E)-beta-damascenone is a character-impact odorant of Elstar and Cox flesh (ref 5); other literature calls its odour cooked-apple-like, but that descriptor was seen only in search snippets for this file, not in a paper read here, so verify before adopting.

suggested_new_tags.label: Fermented / solvent
suggested_new_tags.why: Ethyl acetate (ether/brandy), acetaldehyde (pungent) and fusel alcohols read as fermented or solvent; cider lexicons list 'solvent' and 'vinegary' as distinct descriptors (refs 1, 4, 13). Useful for over-ripe or long-stored fruit; currently forced into 'wine'.
